deep.reconstruction:
Case III of E260: water flows steadily out of a vessel kept full, through a horizontal pipe.

Setup. The vessel is a vertical prism of cross-section ff and height AB = a. The pipe BC has length b and cross-section gg, and the orifice CC has area kk. l = 30 ft is the head of atmospheric pressure, and v is the head due to the efflux velocity. Pressures p are absolute heads, so they include l.

Friction law. Euler's hypothesis is that wall friction per unit length is proportional to the local pressure times perimeter/area, with coefficient alpha. This is a Coulomb-type law, friction proportional to normal pressure.

- In the vertical vessel the velocity is constant, so the balance is dp/dz = 1 - alpha p/f. Integrating from the surface (p = l) to depth a gives p_bottom = f(1 - A_frak)/alpha + A_frak l = A f + A_frak l, where A_frak = e^{-alpha a/f} and A = (1 - A_frak)/alpha.
- At the entrance to the pipe the velocity head changes from v f_frak to v g_frak (f_frak = k^4/f^4, g_frak = k^4/g^4). So p_B = A f + A_frak l + v(f_frak - g_frak).
- The pipe is horizontal, so gravity does no work along it (zeta = 90 deg, cos zeta = 0). Hence dp/dx = -alpha p/g and p_C = B_frak p_B, with B_frak = e^{-alpha b/g}.
- At exit, p_C + v g_frak = l + v.
- Eliminating gives v (1 - B_frak f_frak - (1 - B_frak) g_frak) = A B_frak f - (1 - A_frak B_frak) l. Since (1 - B_frak) = alpha B, this is exactly Euler's formula in §76.

§77 (very wide vessel). Euler sets f_frak = 0 and expands A_frak ≈ 1 - alpha a/f and A ≈ a/f - alpha a^2/(2f^2). This gives v = [a B_frak (1 - alpha a/2f) - (1 - B_frak + alpha a B_frak/f) l] / [1 - (1 - B_frak) g_frak]. Because g_frak <= 1, the denominator equals 1 - g_frak + B_frak g_frak >= B_frak g_frak > 0. Euler reads this as a guarantee that a uniform (steady) regime is reached.

§78 (condition for actual outflow). The numerator must be positive. This is equivalent to B_frak > f l / [f(a + l) - alpha a(a/2 + l)], i.e. e^{alpha b/g} < 1 + a/l - alpha a^2/(2fl) - alpha a/f (continued on p. 368). The next page takes logarithms, giving a critical pipe length b* ≈ (g/alpha) log(1 + a/l) beyond which no water flows. Euler then uses this critical length to measure alpha experimentally.

Purpose. To work out the consequences of Euler's pressure-proportional friction hypothesis for practical hydraulic configurations.
errors: Mixed orders of approximation in §77: A_frak is expanded only to first order in alpha a/f, while A is kept to second order (alpha a^2/2f^2). The discrepancy is of the same order as retained terms, so the final inequality is only first-order consistent. This is harmless numerically.

The last line, as printed in the scan, appears to show the exponent with a minus sign (e^{-alpha b/g} < 1 + a/l ...). Logically the condition B_frak > fl/(...) inverts to e^{+alpha b/g} < 1 + a/l - alpha aa/(2fl) - alpha a/f. If the minus is really printed, it is a typographical slip.

Physical-model issue, not algebraic: friction is made proportional to absolute pressure (including the atmospheric head l). This yields the physically false prediction that a sufficiently long horizontal pipe stops all flow, as stated on the next page. Euler himself flags that gravity within the horizontal tube is ignored.
On the next page (not this one), the correction term should read alpha a(a+2l)/(2f(a+l)), not (a+2f). Either the print or the transcription has an error there.

ideas.what: Friction on a fluid at a wall proportional to local pressure (Coulomb-type law), leading to exponential pressure decay along a horizontal pipe, p_C = p_B e^{-alpha b/g}
ideas.modern_name: Pressure-dependent (Coulomb/Amontons) wall friction; capstan-like exponential attenuation
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler's own E260 hypothesis (later abandoned in hydraulics in favour of velocity-dependent resistance: Chézy, Prony, Darcy-Weisbach)
ideas.where_published: E260, Novi Comment. Petrop. 6 (1756/57, publ. 1761); discussed in Truesdell's introductions to Opera omnia II.12/13 (details unsure)

ideas.what: Pressure in a vertical column with wall friction proportional to pressure saturates: p(z) = (f/alpha)(1 - e^{-alpha z/f}) + p0 e^{-alpha z/f}
ideas.usually_credited_to: H. A. Janssen (1895), for granular media in silos

ideas.what: Steady efflux formula combining Bernoulli velocity-head changes at section changes with exponential frictional pressure losses
ideas.usually_credited_to: Daniel Bernoulli, Euler; head-loss formalism later (Darcy-Weisbach)

ideas.what: Positivity of the denominator as the criterion that a steady (uniform) regime is attained
Critical pipe length beyond which flow ceases, used (next page) to measure the friction coefficient alpha
ideas.modern_name: Threshold (yield-type) flow criterion; inverse determination of a friction coefficient

missed.claim: Euler's pressure in a vertical vessel with friction proportional to pressure has the same form as Janssen's 1895 silo law. Both use wall friction proportional to normal pressure and give exponential saturation toward f/alpha, with alpha playing the role of 4 mu K / D. So Euler's (failed) fluid-friction theory is mathematically an exact anticipation of granular wall-friction statics. Its prediction of flow arrest in long pipes likewise mirrors jamming/arching in granular pipe and hopper flow. I am not aware that historians of granular mechanics cite E260 here.
missed.quote: Ponatur breuitatis ergo A = e^{-alpha a/f}; A = (1-A)/alpha ... v = (A B f - (1 - A B) l)/(1 - B f - alpha B g)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This reframes E260 not as merely wrong hydraulics but as a correct Coulomb-friction continuum model applied to the wrong material. It is a historical precursor for granular-media mechanics (Janssen effect, pressure-dependent rheologies).

deep.surprise_reason: The algebra is routine and correct, and the physical law is known to be wrong for water. The modest interest is the structural identity with the Janssen silo law and with threshold (jamming-like) flow arrest, a connection apparently not made in the literature as far as I know.
transcription_corrections: Final inequality: the exponent should be read (and logically must be) e^{+alpha b/g} < 1 + a/l - alpha aa/(2fl) - ...; the scan's sign over alpha b is ambiguous, and the inequality symbol may be printed as a variant of '<'.
